lead: The threshold voltage V<sub>T</sub> is the gate-to-source voltage at which an nMOS surface just reaches strong inversion. It is a voltage budget: part of the gate voltage cancels the work-function difference and oxide charge, part bends the bands by 2φ<sub>F</sub>, and part holds up the depletion charge. Only gate voltage above V<sub>T</sub> makes channel charge. When the source sits above the body, the depletion region holds more charge and V<sub>T</sub> rises: the body effect. Designers meet it in every stacked transistor and every pass gate.
prereq: You need: the MOS capacitor and inversion at φs = 2φF, from MOS structure; nMOS and pMOS operating regions.

blocks.text: Take an nMOS on a p body with the source tied to the body. Three things must be paid for before inversion charge appears.

items: Flat band. The gate and body materials have different work functions, and the oxide traps some fixed positive charge Qox (C/m²). The gate voltage that makes the bands flat is VFB = φMS − Qox/Cox, where φMS is the gate-to-body work-function difference in volts.
Band bending. The surface potential must rise by 2φF, where φF = (kT/q) ln(NA/ni). At 300 K, kT/q ≈ 0.026 V.
Depletion charge. At φs = 2φF the depletion region holds charge Qdep = √(2qεsiNA·2φF) per unit area. The gate needs Qdep/Cox volts across the oxide to hold it.

blocks.text: Here V<sub>T0</sub> is the threshold with V<sub>SB</sub> = 0; ε<sub>si</sub> ≈ 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁰ F/m is the permittivity of silicon; C<sub>ox</sub> = ε<sub>ox</sub>/t<sub>ox</sub>; N<sub>A</sub> is in m⁻³ when the other quantities are in SI units.

With an n⁺ polysilicon gate, φMS ≈ −(0.56 + φF) V for a p body, so VT0 often comes out close to zero. A shallow threshold-adjust implant of acceptors, dose DI ions per m², adds a sheet of charge at the surface and raises the threshold by ΔVT = qDI/Cox. This is how a process sets VT to the value in its design kit.

Now let the source rise above the body by V<sub>SB</sub> = V<sub>S</sub> − V<sub>B</sub> > 0. The source-body junction is reverse biased, so the surface must reach φ<sub>s</sub> = 2φ<sub>F</sub> + V<sub>SB</sub> before electrons from the source can collect there. The depletion region is wider and holds more charge, so the gate must supply more voltage.

γ is the body-effect coefficient in √V (typically 0.2 to 0.5 √V); heavier doping or a thicker oxide makes it larger. The rise is fastest at small V<sub>SB</sub> and grows only as a square root later. When source and body are tied, V<sub>SB</sub> = 0 and the effect vanishes.

In a two-input NAND, the lower nMOS has its source at ground, but the upper nMOS has its source at the node between them. When that node rises, the upper transistor has V<sub>SB</sub> > 0, a higher V<sub>T</sub> and less current. An nMOS pass gate is hit the same way: as its output (its source) rises, V<sub>T</sub> rises too, so the weak 1 it passes is lower than V<sub>DD</sub> − V<sub>T0</sub>.

For a pMOS in an n-well the same terms appear with opposite signs: V<sub>Tp</sub> is negative, the body effect makes |V<sub>Tp</sub>| larger when the well sits above the source (V<sub>BS</sub> > 0), and the formula uses |φ<sub>F</sub>|, the donor doping N<sub>D</sub> and V<sub>BS</sub> in place of V<sub>SB</sub>.

Temperature lowers |VT| by roughly 1 to 2 mV per kelvin, because φF shrinks as ni grows. Mobility also falls with temperature, so at high gate voltage the current drops when hot, while leakage near threshold rises. Channel length and drain voltage shift VT too; those short-channel changes are in MOSFET scaling and short-channel effects.
In the SPICE Level 1 model the threshold is carried by VTO (V<sub>T0</sub>), GAMMA (γ), PHI (2φ<sub>F</sub>) and TOX (t<sub>ox</sub>).

examples.question: An nMOS has N<sub>A</sub> = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³, t<sub>ox</sub> = 4 nm, an n⁺ polysilicon gate and fixed oxide charge Q<sub>ox</sub>/q = 2 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻². Use ε<sub>ox</sub> = 3.45 × 10⁻¹¹ F/m, ε<sub>si</sub> = 1.04 × 10⁻¹⁰ F/m, n<sub>i</sub> = 1.5 × 10¹⁰ cm⁻³, kT/q = 0.026 V and φ<sub>MS</sub> = −(0.56 + φ<sub>F</sub>) V. (a) Find V<sub>T0</sub>. (b) What threshold-adjust dose raises it to 0.45 V?
steps: Units: N<sub>A</sub> = 10¹⁷ cm⁻³ = 10²³ m⁻³; Q<sub>ox</sub> = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ × 2 × 10¹⁴ m⁻² = 3.2 × 10⁻⁵ C/m².
examples.answer: V<sub>T0</sub> ≈ 0.036 V, almost zero; a boron dose of about 2.2 × 10¹² cm⁻² raises it to 0.45 V.

examples.question: The adjusted device of the first example (V<sub>T0</sub> = 0.45 V, N<sub>A</sub> = 10²³ m⁻³, C<sub>ox</sub> = 8.625 × 10⁻³ F/m², 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.8171 V) is the upper transistor of a stack, with its source 1 V above the body. Find γ, the new V<sub>T</sub>, and the fall in saturation current at V<sub>GS</sub> = 1.2 V using I<sub>D</sub> ∝ (V<sub>GS</sub> − V<sub>T</sub>)².
examples.answer: γ = 0.21 √V; V<sub>T</sub> rises from 0.45 V to 0.544 V; the saturation current falls by about 23 %.

traps: Use V<sub>SB</sub> = V<sub>S</sub> − V<sub>B</sub> under the root, positive for reverse bias in an nMOS. Putting in V<sub>BS</sub> = −1 V gives √(2φ<sub>F</sub> − 1), which is not even real when 2φ<sub>F</sub> < 1 V.
The formula has 2φ<sub>F</sub>, not φ<sub>F</sub>, in both the bending term and the square roots.
γ has units √V; γ × √V gives volts.
Keep N<sub>A</sub> in m⁻³ with q, ε<sub>si</sub> and C<sub>ox</sub> in SI units; mixing cm⁻³ in gives answers off by 10³.
Body effect is zero only when source and body are at the same voltage; in a stack, only the bottom transistor is free of it.

quiz.q: Write V<sub>T0</sub> for an nMOS and name its three parts.
quiz.a: V<sub>T0</sub> = V<sub>FB</sub> + 2φ<sub>F</sub> + √(2qε<sub>si</sub>N<sub>A</sub>·2φ<sub>F</sub>)/C<sub>ox</sub>: the flat-band voltage, the band bending to strong inversion, and the voltage across the oxide that holds the depletion charge.

quiz.q: Why does reverse source-body bias raise V<sub>T</sub>?
quiz.a: The surface must reach 2φ<sub>F</sub> + V<sub>SB</sub> before inversion, so the depletion region is wider and holds more charge; the gate needs more voltage to support it.

quiz.q: V<sub>T0</sub> = 0.5 V, γ = 0.30 √V, 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.80 V and V<sub>SB</sub> = 2 V. Find V<sub>T</sub>.
C<sub>ox</sub> = 8.625 × 10⁻³ F/m². What implant dose in cm⁻² raises V<sub>T</sub> by 0.2 V?
In a two-input nMOS NAND pull-down with both inputs high, which transistor shows body effect, and what does it do to the falling output?
quiz.a: The upper one: its source sits at the middle node, above the grounded body, so its V<sub>T</sub> rises and it conducts less. The output falls more slowly than with two identical unbiased transistors.

quiz.q: A student puts V<sub>BS</sub> = −1 V in place of V<sub>SB</sub> into √(2φ<sub>F</sub> + V) with 2φ<sub>F</sub> = 0.8 V. What goes wrong?
quiz.a: The root becomes √(0.8 − 1) = √(−0.2), not a real number, so no threshold can be found. With the correct V<sub>SB</sub> = +1 V the root is √1.8 and V<sub>T</sub> rises, as reverse bias must.

beyond: Compact models such as BSIM add non-uniform doping, short-channel terms and back-gate coefficients to this formula. Fully depleted silicon-on-insulator processes use a back-gate bias to move V<sub>T</sub> on purpose, trading speed for leakage while the chip runs. Search for "body biasing FD-SOI" and "multi-threshold CMOS" to see the idea in use.

figure.caption: Threshold voltage of the worked device as its source rises above the body. At V<sub>SB</sub> = 1 V the body effect has added 0.094 V; each further volt adds less (0.070 V, then 0.058 V).

spec.aria: Plot of threshold voltage against source-to-body voltage from 0 to 3 volts for gamma 0.21 root volt: 0.450, 0.544, 0.614 and 0.672 volts at 0, 1, 2 and 3 volts.
